brionali .

vegetazione nel
l'embrione d'un seme
maturo . Gli
involucri
del seme
sono
destinati a proteggere l'embrione dal contatto dei corpi esterni
e
di
preservarlo dal disseccamento e dall'alterazione
fino al
momento che il seme affidato al terreno non si trovi in con
dizione da poter germogliare e vegetare.
L'embrione
allora
trova nel seme,
se esso è munito d'un perispermo,
il primo
alimento che
conviene alla delicatezza della
sua organizza
zione. Nel caso che il perispermo manchi , l'embrione si trova
provvisto d'un deposito di sostanza nutritiva (o cotiledoni) che
sotto l'influenza del calore e dell'umidità si trasforma in una
materia lattiginosa assimilabile
che non differisce punto da
quella del perispermo.
Le trasformazioni chimiche, dice Richard, che hanno luogo
nell'embrione nei
corso della germinazione, sono ancora ma
lamente conosciute. Un seme per germogliare ha bisogno d'una
quantità
di
ossigeno eguale a 1/8 circa del suo volume ;
per
cui una parte d'ossigeno su tre o quattro d'azoto sono le pro
porzioni più favorevoli per la germinazione .

the only means
of
preserving them is that
of
burying them in the vi
scera of the earth. Twenty years
ago
I
cultivated in open
ground
the
Datura,
the Capsicum,
the Solanum
and
the Hyoscyamus;
above
the ground
where
these plants had been cultivated, there
was
made a large
deposit
of
rubble or broken stone;
after
17 years these fillings were removed, and
the seeds of the Solanaceae,
fallen
to the ground, saw the light again, some sprang up and pro
duced great abundance of fruit beyond description, espe
cially one
plant
of
Solanum lycopersicum or common Tomato,
which counted the fabulous figure of 67 fruits; there also appeared a
gigantic plant of black Henbane, with leaves of the size
of
those of the Acanthus,
brought about 20 spikes
of
fruit,
of which, the terminal (60 centimeters long) contained 90.
All these Solanaceae, born by chance,
were vigorous,
because the embryos so wonderfully preserved
in the
viscera
of the earth,
had undergone
no alteration
in the
vicissitudes of the seasons,
and consequently there had not
been able
to take place
the aforementioned
atrophy
of
some
parts of
the em
bryo.
To be convinced
of what I have stated it is necessary
that one take a quick look at germination, one of the most im
portant parts of plant physiology.
Germination is the first stage of
vegetation in the
embryo of a mature
seed. The
involucres
of the seed
are
destined to protect the embryo from contact with external objects
and
to preserve it from drying out and alteration
until
the moment the seed entrusted to the ground finds itself in con
ditions to be able to germinate and vegetate.
The embryo
then
finds in the seed,
if it is provided with a perisperm,
the first
food that
is suitable for the delicacy of
its organisa
tion. In the case that the perisperm is lacking, the embryo finds
itself provided with a deposit of nutritive substance (or cotyledons) that
under the influence of heat and humidity transforms into a
milky substance assimilable
which differs in no way from
that of the perisperm.
The chemical transformations, says Richard, that take place
in the embryo during
the course of germination, are still only
poorly understood. A seed to germinate needs a
quantity
of
oxygen equal to about 1/8 of its volume;
for
this reason a part of oxygen to three or four parts of nitrogen are the pro
portions most favorable for germination.

The varieties of Tomatoes presented at the recent Special Exhibition
of Fruit
and
Vegetables
by Mr. Giovanni Giovannini,
Agent at Collodi, attracted the attention of the public not only,
but of those knowledgeable and cultivators of vegetables.
Having been provided with some information regarding
the respective merits of the 19 va
rieties exhibited, we have
thought it pleasing
to our
readers
to
publish them
in the
Bulletin.
Now that thanks to the
courageous initiative of Cav. Cirio and other
few well-deserving
individuals, the export trade of Vegetables and Fruit
becomes ever larger, it is absolutely necessary that
our Gardeners and Fruit Growers learn

Thus, the 2nd Class medal was granted to the first, and that of 3rd Class to the latter.

The Tomatoes that are ordinarily cultivated at the Cascine belong to those varieties that find a market outlet, although all other varieties have also been cultivated both in form and in color, but which for now remain either in the gardens or on the counters of the greengrocers. An excellent tomato is that which we call at the Cascine del Montagni, having been favored with the seed by Mr. Luigi Montagni, Gardener to Marchese Ridolfi at Bibbiani. Good is also the dwarf variety of Paris, known by the name of also without stake.

Among the Peppers, besides the border varieties and those to be pickled, three varieties are cultivated that are highly sought after on the market, especially that: large yellow of Spain. The others are the red heart of ox and the red hare's snout, both of which are excellent cooked and dressed in salad.

All the varieties of petonciani that were known have had to yield place to a new variety that bears the name of Long Violet Petonciano. This is much more delicate in flavor than the others, yields a large crop, and adapts very well to our soils.

One of the collections, which has had more failures than the others, is that of Turnips. Almost fifty varieties were experimented with at the Cascine, but of these only nine withstood the test for various reasons, either due to low yield, or inferior merit, or because they do not find a market outlet. Those that are worthy of cultivation are the following:

Yellow Turnip or Golden Ball
White with entire leaves
of Limousin
Round of Vertus
Long of Vertus
Early flat red
Red
Early flat white
White of Norfolk.

The Roots experimented with have been many and almost all have succeeded. The best are always the oldest, namely, the white and round pink, the white and half-long pink, the pink of China, the scarlet round and half-long. The early round gray, the long black winter, the gray of Laon are good roots, although a bit harder and more ordinary than the others.
